title: ‘Digger’ is a Box Office Flop. It Might Be the Most Relevant Film of the Year
gist: WIRED (Middle East) review argues Iñárritu's Digger, a box-office flop starring Tom Cruise, is the year's most relevant film: a satire of an oil tycoon causing a climate catastrophe, framed as a play funded by a surveillance-company heir who profits from the disaster, skewering tech moguls' growing grip on culture.

insights.claim: Alejandro González Iñárritu's Digger, a Tom Cruise satire about an oil baron whose drilling sends an iceberg toward Europe, had an underwhelming box-office opening and is hard to market because its key reveals are spoilers.
insights.speaker: Carla Sertin
insights.so_what: Ambitious, hard-to-market satire continues to underperform theatrically.
insights.quote: despite an underwhelming opening at the box office, this sprawling, grotesque satire may be the most relevant film of the year.
insights.locator: The trailer for Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Digger

insights.claim: The film satirizes political leaders who shrug at a climate disaster's death toll but overreact to its financial cost.
insights.speaker: Carla Sertin
insights.so_what: Reflects popular cynicism toward political handling of climate risk.
insights.locator: This context comes in bits and pieces

insights.claim: The reviewer argues that today's tech moguls are increasingly seeking cultural clout and that culture is now distributed through technology, citing Jeff Bezos owning Prime Video, Apple's Apple TV and algorithmic social platforms as gatekeepers.
insights.speaker: Carla Sertin
insights.so_what: Concentration of cultural distribution in big tech gives platforms narrative power and content-market leverage.
insights.quote: The tech moguls of today are increasingly seeking cultural clout, and culture is now largely dispersed through technology: Jeff Bezos owns Prime Video; Apple has Apple TV.
insights.locator: His decision to fund a play

insights.claim: In the film, a surveillance-company heir funds a cathartic satire to deflect blame onto a past villain while profiting from the ongoing catastrophe, which the reviewer reads as commentary on how patrons use art to placate audiences.
insights.speaker: Carla Sertin
insights.so_what: Frames 'catharsis as deflection', a lens for evaluating corporate-sponsored culture and ESG messaging.
insights.quote: it’s a deflection, placating the audience by giving them a villain in the past so they can accept the present, while he profits off of the catastrophe the play satirizes.
insights.locator: Kenny also isn’t putting on the play
